nameStory: This stonecrop gets its scientific name from Russian botanist Alexander Tatarinow, who collected plants in China and Mongolia in the 1800s. Like other members of the stonecrop family, it's called a "stonecrop" because these tough succulents can literally grow in the cracks of stones and rocky places where other plants would wither.
description: Tatarinow's stonecrop is a hardy succulent perennial that forms low, spreading clumps about 6-12 inches tall and wide. Its thick, fleshy blue-green leaves store water like tiny reservoirs, helping it survive in tough conditions. In late summer, it produces clusters of small star-shaped flowers that are typically white to pale pink. This Asian native is extremely rare in New England, likely appearing only as an occasional garden escape.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Thick, fleshy blue-green leaves that feel cool and firm to the touch, arranged alternately along the stems - squeeze gently and they feel like little water balloons

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white to pale pink star-shaped flowers with 5 pointed petals, clustered in flat-topped groups at stem tips in late summer

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing succulent that spreads by underground stems, forming dense mats rarely taller than a foot

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Sturdy, smooth stems that are often reddish-tinged and feel firm and waxy to the touch

habitat: [UNCERTAIN - Limited information available] Likely found in well-drained, sunny locations such as rock gardens, sandy soils, or disturbed areas where it may have escaped cultivation. As a succulent adapted to dry conditions, it would favor spots with good drainage and full sun exposure.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as small rosettes of blue-green succulent leaves. Plants are low and inconspicuous but the distinctive thick, waxy leaves are already apparent.
seasonality.summer: Foliage is at its fullest, with thick blue-green leaves clearly visible. Flower buds begin forming in late summer as flat-topped clusters.
seasonality.fall: Peak flowering time with clusters of small white to pale pink star-shaped blooms. Seeds develop after flowers fade.
seasonality.winter: In milder areas, some leaves may persist, but most top growth dies back, with the plant surviving underground until spring.

funFact: This plant is so tough that in its native Asian habitat, it can survive being completely frozen solid in winter and bounce back to life when it thaws - its cells have special antifreeze-like compounds that prevent fatal ice crystal damage!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other stonecrops in gardens, especially Orpine or Butterfly Stonecrop. Look for the blue-green leaf color and smaller stature - Tatarinow's stonecrop stays much lower and more compact than the taller garden stonecrops.
contextualKnowledge: With only one recorded observation in New England, this is an extremely rare find that's likely a garden escape rather than an established population. Most stonecrop identifications in New England will be the more common Orpine or other garden varieties.
compareHints: Compared to the common Orpine found throughout New England, Tatarinow's stonecrop is much smaller and more compact, staying under a foot tall versus Orpine's 1-3 foot height. Its leaves are more blue-green than the gray-green of Orpine, and it lacks the dense, showy pink flower clusters that make Orpine so noticeable in late summer.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Orpine differs from other stonecrops in its much larger size and robust growth habit - while most stonecrops are low, creeping plants, orpine stands tall and upright.
Pink Mongolian stonecrop differs from its New England relatives like orpine and garden stonecrop by its trailing, mat-forming habit and distinctive blue-gray leaves.
Garden stonecrop differs from its close relative orpine by having more distinctly spoon-shaped leaves and typically paler flowers.
Butterfly stonecrop is larger and showier than its relatives, reaching 2 feet tall versus the 6-12 inches of most other stonecrops in New England.
Great Stonecrop is much larger and more robust than its close relative Orpine, with bigger leaves and flower clusters.
